Research – a systematic inquiry or investigation into a topic – is conducted across the curricula at the University at Albany. Whether it is using ancient texts or more recent diaries to develop new understandings or analyzing data to find mathematical patterns, research is an important component of your university education. Research begins with a question. What answer will you uncover?
Languages, Literatures & Cultures
What is Languages Research?
Linguistics: learn more about the structure of a specific language, its history, variation in how it is used today, and ways to teach and learn it
Literatures: study aspects of human experience explored in literary works and learn to interpret them critically
Cultures: learn more about different cultures and study ways to characterize and teach them and to make global connections
How can I do research in languages at UAlbany?
- Work with faculty on an on-going project
- Carry out research as part of an advanced course
For example, in a course on «Franco-American French », students used Professor Cynthia Fox’s corpus of sociolinguistic interviews to conduct original research on the lexicon of Franco-American French.
- Participate in the honors program and write an honors thesis

Taquile is an island in the middle of Lake Titicaca, a couple hour boat ride from Puno. The Quechua speaking island, though frequently visited by tourists, still retains a very traditional lifestyle, which includes weaving, traditional food and dress, and mythology. The beautifully illustrated book, Kusikiy: A Child From Taquile, Peru by Mercedes Cecilia, offers spectacular insight into the ancient culture still living on this fascinating island.
Children’s books have a way of simplifying unfamiliar ideas and ways of life. Through the story of the young boy Kusikiy, we learn how the islanders of Taquile live. In the tale, Kusikiy learns from his great-grandfather that a constellation is missing from the sky. He asks the APU, the spirit for the glaciers for help, and an adventure ensues that walks us through an array of traditions. We learn the importance of the giant frogs, condors, and flamingos found around and in the high altitude lake. We learn about the stone terraces that continue to decorate the island. We learn how to weave memories into wool

claim.title: Colorado/Denver local-entity neuron with non-Colorado contact/number suppression
claim.lede: The positive pole is dominated by Colorado/Denver/Boulder place references and by nearby spaces, punctuation, dates, phone/address fragments, and institutional boilerplate when the preceding context establishes a Colorado frame (e.g., Colorado Department of Education, University of Colorado, Colorado State University, Denver datelines, 9NEWS, C.R.S. citations). The same kind of numeric/contact/citation string is often strongly negative when it belongs to another state or non-Colorado administrative context. Thus numbers, addresses, and legal hyphens are not the core cue by themselves: they inherit the sign of the surrounding place/entity context. Strong examples often place the marked token on a space or number immediately after a Colorado institution or before a Colorado date/phone number, so the cue can be earlier and not at the marked token. The negative pole is best explained as suppression of non-Colorado regional/administrative/contact/citation material and other-state natural-heritage/geographic labels, not as a general “not-Colorado” topic detector. Some exceptions remain: ‘Colorado Plateaus’ in a geological context is negative, showing that exact string ‘Colorado’ is not sufficient without a Colorado-state/entity frame.
claim.what_would_change_my_mind: I would revise this if a random sample of clearly Colorado-state/Denver/Boulder contexts (including the token-level occurrences of ‘Colorado’, ‘Denver’, ‘Boulder’) often failed to be positive, or if non-Colorado phone/address/citation blocks were as often positive as Colorado ones. The explanation would also need narrowing if high positive responses occurred on arbitrary numbers/spaces without any preceding Colorado entity, or if high negative responses occurred on arbitrary numbers regardless of non-Colorado place/administrative context. If ‘Colorado Plateaus’ and other non-state uses of ‘Colorado’ were reliably positive, I would change P1 from a state/entity feature to a pure string feature; if ‘Alaska Natural Heritage’ were positive when no numeric/contact cue is present, I would weaken N1/N3 and favor a more general non-Colorado-region suppression account.
claim.one_paragraph: Strong positive activation when the context names Colorado, Denver, Boulder, or close metonyms/derivatives such as CO, Colo, CU, Broncos, Centennial State. The marked token is often a nearby space, punctuation mark, ‘at’, ‘is’, or a following numeral, but the preceding context contains the place/entity. Exact ‘Colorado’ and ‘Denver’ are among the strongest tokens (mean products about 94–99); Boulder, CU, Aspen, Pueblo, and Springs are weaker unless clearly in a Colorado frame. Non-matches: generic place strings and non-Colorado states do not fire; ‘Colorado Plateaus’ in a purely geological context can even be negative. Very strong responses on spaces/punctuation/phone or citation numbers adjacent to Colorado institutions and local boilerplate: e.g., ‘Colorado Department of Education… § 22-5-119, C.R.S.’, ‘University of Colorado… 720-848-18…’, ‘Colorado State University Extension… .colostate.edu/pubs…’, ‘DENVER — …’, ‘9NEWS’, ‘Colorado Women’s Education Foundation’. Matches samples 58669917, 68975890, 45930664, 3530404, 71837166, 18774120. Similar phone/address/statute strings without a Colorado frame tend to be negative, so the combination with a Colorado entity is required. High when a Colorado-related historical/state fact is being enumerated and the marked token is a space, date, number, or following word: ‘Colorado became the thirty-eighth state… Its nickname is the Centennial State’ and ‘Colorado Labor Wars, 1903–1904’ are positive. The pattern needs the Colorado frame; bare dates, numbers, or historical lists in other states are weak or negative. Inside Colorado-focused documents, contact blocks and URLs often produce high activation at the space or digit adjacent to the number: e.g., a clinic at ‘720-848-18…’, a school contact at ‘1-877-545-…’, a CSU extension URL ending ‘/06703.html’, and local-media marker ‘9NEWS’. This is a specific subtype of P2; non-Colorado contact blocks (North Dakota, Nevada, Utah) with the same numeric/punctuation shape are negative. Terms like Boulder, Rocky Mountain, Aspen, Pueblo, Springs, and Denver Broncos can be positive, but many are weaker or context-dependent. They fire strongly when the preceding context places them in Colorado (e.g., University of Colorado Boulder, Rocky Mountain National Park, Colorado Springs); they are not reliably positive when the same word belongs to another state, a generic geological term, or only a broad western topic. This explains why ‘Rocky’, ‘Aspen’, and ‘Spring’ show lower hit fractions than ‘Colorado’ and ‘Denver’.
claim.negative_pole: Strong negative in contexts dominated by another state or region and its administrative/contact material: North Dakota Department of Agriculture phone/address, ND Game and Fish contact, Elko/Nevada phone/address, Utah/Zion phone number, Alaska Natural Heritage Program, Qinghai area/administrative figures. Matches 32442428, 42760175, 13854828, 74647570, 3819061, 33203795. The same phone/address/citation shape in a Colorado frame is positive, so non-Colorado framing plus contact/administrative material is the repeated negative pattern. Very negative on long phone numbers, ZIP/address fragments, statute/legal citations, grant IDs, and area/statistical figures when no Colorado entity supports them: e.g., Qinghai ‘278,400 square miles’, a Bismarck ND phone number, ‘N.D.C.C. § 28-33-02’, Qinghai grant ‘No. 2016-ZJ-…’, Utah/Greyhound phone numbers. Ordinary numbers away from such blocks are only weakly negative, so this is not a simple number detector; the negative response needs the non-Colorado contact/citation/administrative context. Negative for labels such as ‘Alaska Natural Heritage Program’, ‘Dakota’, ‘Nevada’, ‘Wild’, ‘Natural’, and ‘Spring’ when they are not in a Colorado frame. Strong at Alaska Natural Heritage Program (Natural -37.75), and negative token statistics include Dakota, Alaska, Nevada, Wild, Natural, Heritage, Spring, Cascade, Tahoe, Moj. Similar Colorado natural/outdoor terms can be positive via Colorado entity context, so the cue is other-state branding rather than the topic of nature/heritage. Negative at commas, spaces, or words near non-Colorado geographic superlatives and descriptions: ‘highest point solely in Nevada is 13,063-foot Wheeler Peak’ (comma after 13), ‘Loktak Lake, the largest freshwater lake of North East India’ (comma after Lake), ‘highest peak in Canada…’ and similar passages. General geography alone is not enough; a non-Colorado place plus superlative/number/description often produces the strong negative. Strong negative in Qinghai/Xinjiang/Tibet/India administrative-geography contexts, especially area figures, administrative divisions, and grant/citation strings: 33203795, 33203820, 73735612, 19148625. This overlaps N1/N2 but is distinctive enough to note: the neuron suppresses these non-Colorado, non-US administrative details; the isolated presence of the word ‘Colorado’ as a geological province in another passage does not rescue it.

output.title: Colorado/Denver local-entity neuron with narrow numeric/contact suppression
output.lede: Positive activation is organized around explicit Colorado, Denver, or Boulder entities and the spaces, numbers, punctuation, addresses, citations, and local-news or institutional boilerplate that inherit that frame. The negative pole is much narrower than “non-Colorado”: broad other-state administrative, natural, and geographic contexts often fail or turn positive. Supported negative cues are dense unanchored numeric/contact/legal or address blocks and a narrow other-state “Natural Heritage” label; several strong unrelated responses remain unresolved.

positive.name: Colorado/Denver/Boulder state and city referent
positive.description: Strong positive activation when the prefix names Colorado, Denver, Boulder, or close metonyms such as CO, Colo, CU, Broncos, or Centennial State. The marked token is often a nearby space, punctuation mark, “at”, “is”, or following numeral, but the preceding context contains the place/entity. Exact place tokens are strongest; weaker toponyms need an explicit Colorado frame. Generic place strings, non-Colorado states, and purely geological “Colorado Plateaus” uses without a state/entity frame do not reliably fire.

positive.name: Colorado institution, dateline, local-news, and legal boilerplate adjacency
positive.description: Very strong responses occur on spaces, punctuation, phone or citation numbers adjacent to Colorado institutions and local boilerplate: “DENVER —”, “Colorado Department of Education… § … C.R.S.”, “University of Colorado… 720…”, “Colorado State University Extension… colostate.edu”, “9NEWS”, “Colorado Women’s Education Foundation”. The Colorado entity must be present in the prefix; a bare phone, address, or statute string is not sufficient.

positive.name: Colorado dates, state-history facts, and enumerations
positive.description: High when a Colorado-related historical or state fact is being enumerated and the marked token is a space, date, number, or following word: “Colorado became the thirty-eighth state… Its nickname is the Centennial State” and “Colorado Labor Wars, 1903–1904” are positive. The pattern needs the Colorado frame; bare dates, numbers, or historical lists in other states are weak or negative.

positive.name: Colorado local contact/address/phone/URL blocks
positive.description: Inside a Colorado-focused document, contact blocks and URLs often produce high activation at the space or digit adjacent to the number: a clinic at “720-848-18…”, a school contact at “1-877-545-…”, a CSU extension URL ending “.html”, and the local-media marker “9NEWS”. Revised condition: only when an explicit Colorado/Denver/Boulder institution, place, or local-news dateline is already in the prefix. A bare 720/303 number or generic contact block is not enough.

positive.name: Weaker Colorado outdoor and Front Range toponyms
positive.description: Under a Colorado frame, terms such as Boulder, Rocky Mountain, Aspen, Pueblo, Springs, and Denver Broncos can be positive, especially in University of Colorado Boulder, Rocky Mountain National Park, and Colorado Springs phrasing. They are not reliable when the same word belongs to another state, a generic geological term, or only a broad western topic; use this rule only in combination with explicit Colorado/Boulder/Denver support.

negative.name: Unanchored dense numeric, contact, citation, and address blocks
negative.description: Strong negative at the central punctuation/digit of dense identifier strings—telephone groups with parentheses or hyphens, ZIP/address fragments, statute/legal citations of the “§ 28-33-02” type, grant IDs, and long comma-grouped area or statistical figures—when the prefix lacks a Colorado/Denver/Boulder entity or local Colorado frame. The sign attaches to the whole formatted block, often at a space, comma, hyphen, parenthesis, or single digit. Ordinary dates, small counts, email-only contact labels, and geographically nonspecific numbers are weak or unreliable; a Colorado entity plus contact/citation can reverse this to positive under P2/P4.

negative.name: Non-Colorado “Natural Heritage” program label
negative.description: Negative for the capitalized label or adjacent token in an other-state natural-heritage program name such as “Alaska Natural Heritage Program” when it is outside a Colorado frame. This does not generalize to nature, wildlife, parks, outdoor recreation, rivers, mountains, or other-state geography: many such non-Colorado natural and geographical passages are positive or neutral. The cue is the program-label construction, not the topic of natural heritage.

output.what_would_change_my_mind: I would broaden the negative pole again only if broad non-Colorado administrative, natural, or geographic contexts reliably and strongly predicted negative responses; the measured feedback shows many such contexts are positive, so those rules were narrowed or withdrawn. I would weaken P2/P4 if Colorado institutions with nearby phone/address/citation blocks often failed to be positive, or if bare numeric blocks without any Colorado frame were as often positive. I would revise N2 if dense phone, statute, grant, address, or comma-grouped area figures were frequently positive without a Colorado entity. I would drop N3 if other-state “Natural Heritage” program labels were consistently positive. Strong unexplained positive or negative responses in unrelated political, cultural, or historical contexts remain unresolved unless a recurring contextual pattern is found.
